newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura woes highlight criminals' shadow over Japan.
newsitem.headline: Nomura woes highlight criminals' shadow over Japan.

text.p: A police raid on Nomura Securities on Tuesday underscored the long, dark shadow organised crime casts on Japanese businesses despite more than a decade of efforts to curb gang-connected racketeers.

Japanese prosecutors said a director at Nomura Securities illegally paid 38 million yen ($309,000) to a company run by a relative of a "sokaiya" racketeer to avoid disruption of one of Nomura's annual shareholders' meetings.

Police have said Sokaiya, self-styled "professional shareholders" often linked to Japan's "yakuza" crime syndicates, gain the right to attend shareholder meetings by acquiring a small amount of a firm's stock. They then try to extort money by threatening to expose dubious business practices, police have said.

Companies have also been known to hire them to muzzle legitimate shareholders' questions and ensure annual shareholders meetings end smoothly and quickly. Some firms hire racketeers to ward off the attacks of others.
Paying off sokaiya became illegal under changes to Japan's Commercial Code in 1982.
But over the past year Kirin Brewery, prestigious department store Takashimaya and seasoning maker Ajinomoto either admitted to or were under investigation for making such payments.
Takashimaya's president resigned to take responsibility for three executives' payments to sokaiya, and police have arrested two Ajinomoto executives and a Kirin official on similiar charges.

To avoid harassment by sokaiya, leading listed firms have resorted to holding their annual shareholders meetings on the same day in late June to make it difficult for racketeers to attend the meetings in force.
To make their point, however, racketeers have used resourcefulness and adaptability -- and violence.

In February 1994, Fuji Photo executive Juntaro Suzuki, whose duties included dealing with sokaiya, was stabbed to death outside his apartment in central Japan. He was one of three executives to die in mob-linked attacks after Japan implemented an anti-gangster law in 1992.
"Involvement with the underworld is not something that brokerages have a monopoly on," one financial analyst told Reuters.
"In the banking industry, the real estate industry, at corporations in general, it is very much a part of doing business in Japan."

Ties between financial firms and yakuza grabbed attention last year when the government budgeted taxpayers' money to help wind up failed mortgage firms -- a hefty chunk of whose bad loans officials themselves said involved organised crime money.

The alleged role of gangsters at Japan's harbours has also been whispered as one factor foiling resolution of a U.S.-Japan dispute over port practices, in which Washington has said it will impose trade sanctions on Japanese shipping companies next month.
